tts: Story one. In France, a supermarket chain has been selling ugly fruit and vegetables at a discount, to raise awareness of food waste. The aim was to highlight the fact that millions of tonnes of food are wasted every year because buyers refuse to buy odd-shaped produce. Customers were invited to blind-taste both kinds and admitted that they tasted exactly the same. The supermarket claims the campaign was a success: everything sold out within three days, and customer numbers rose by twenty-four per cent.

Story two. A new species of monkey has been discovered in the forests of Myanmar. Conservationists based in Cambridge made the discovery after hunters reported seeing a monkey unlike anything else in the area. The monkeys have a wide, turned-up nose which fills with water when it rains. Local people assured the conservationists that the monkeys would be easy to locate, because whenever it rained they could be heard sneezing.

Story three. In Norway, two teenagers found cash worth eighty-one thousand dollars in a bag on a train and handed it in. Police praised them for their honesty, but the teenagers denied acting heroically, pointing out that the cash was not theirs and that it had not occurred to them to keep it.

items.q: What do the three stories have in common?
o: They all took place in France

items.q: What did the supermarket customers admit?
o: The ugly and the standard fruit tasted the same

items.q: How can the new monkeys be located?
o: They can be heard sneezing when it rains

tts: All the ugly fruit and vegetables were sold out within three days, and the number of customers rose by twenty-four per cent during that period. The supermarket has announced that it is now looking at rolling the campaign out across all its stores in France.

The monkeys spend rainy days sitting with their heads between their knees to avoid the water. Although the discovery of a new species is exciting, conservationists have warned that these monkeys were already on the endangered species list.

The money in Norway belonged to an elderly man who had left the bag on the seat. The bag also contained his passport. The teenagers called the police immediately to inform them that they had found it. Police were unable to confirm whether the teenagers had received a reward.

items.s: The ugly produce sold out within three days.
Customer numbers fell during the campaign.
The monkeys were already on the endangered species list.
The bag in Norway contained a passport as well as cash.
The police confirmed that the teenagers were rewarded.

acts.title: Choosing the verb that carries the meaning
rule: “He said that…” reports the words. A reporting verb reports the act: whether the speaker was conceding, refusing, insisting or merely asserting. At B2 the difficulty is not the meaning but the pattern, because every one of these verbs takes a different structure and none of them can be guessed.
points: admit, claim, argue, deny, insist, point out, announce, confirm, explain.
admit, deny, suggest, recommend. He denied copying it.
remind, invite, persuade, warn, tell. She reminded him to email.
refuse, offer, promise, threaten, claim. She refused to eat it.
assure, inform, remind, tell. He assured them that it was safe.
insist takes on with an -ing form, or that with a clause.
eg: He admitted that he had driven carelessly.
They claimed the campaign had been a success.
She claimed to have lost the certificate.
He reminded her to email him.
They assured the conservationists that it would be easy.
She pointed out that the cash was not theirs.
He insisted on paying for everybody.
acts.careful: “He denied to copy it” and “She suggested me to come” are both wrong. deny and suggest never take an infinitive; suggest takes that or -ing.

write.q: Write about 180 words summarizing a disagreement you have read about or witnessed — a dispute at work, a story in the news, an argument in your building. Report what each side said using at least five different reporting verbs, and use at least three different patterns. Do not use “said” more than once.
plan: what the other admitted or denied
write.model:
The dispute in our building was about a tree, and it lasted four months.

The ground-floor owner claimed to have obtained permission to remove it, and produced a document nobody could read. The three flats above pointed out that the document was dated 2011 and referred to a different tree.

He then admitted that the permission might not apply, but insisted on cutting the lower branches anyway, on the grounds that they touched his window. Two neighbours denied that they had ever touched anything, and one of them photographed the gap to prove it.

The management company assured everybody that they would investigate, and then did not. The council, when finally asked, confirmed that the tree was protected and that removing it would cost more than the flat.

The tree is still there. Nobody has mentioned it since March, and the ground-floor owner has fitted a blind.
